lesson.title: Range: The Fastest, Least Forgiving Measure of Spread
lesson.summary: The range measures the spread of a data set as the difference between its maximum and minimum values; it is quick to compute but extremely sensitive to outliers because it depends entirely on the two most extreme observations.
lesson.body:
Spread describes how tightly or loosely the values in a distribution are packed around their center, and the range is the simplest possible way to measure it. The range is defined as the maximum value in a data set minus the minimum value. If a class's quiz scores run from 62 to 98, the range is 98 minus 62, or 36 points. This single number tells you the width of the entire interval the data cover, from the smallest observation to the largest.

The range's simplicity is also its biggest weakness. Unlike measures that use every observation in some way, the range depends on exactly two data points: the maximum and the minimum. Every other value in the data set, no matter how many observations there are, has zero influence on the range. This makes the range even less resistant than the mean, because at least the mean incorporates information from every observation; the range ignores everything except the two most extreme points, which are precisely the values most likely to be outliers.

Consider two versions of a small data set of measurements: 12, 15, 18, 20, and 22. The range here is 22 minus 12, or 10. Now suppose a sixth measurement of 95 is added because of an equipment glitch. The new range is 95 minus 12, or 83, more than eight times larger than before, even though only one of six values changed and the other five stayed exactly where they were. A single unusual value more than eightfolded the apparent spread of the data, while a resistant measure of spread built from the middle of the data would barely have noticed the glitch at all.

This sensitivity means the range is best treated as a quick, rough first look at spread rather than a reliable summary on its own. It answers the question of how wide the interval covered by all the data is, which is genuinely useful when you care about worst case or best case values, such as the coldest and hottest temperatures ever recorded at a location, or the shortest and longest wait times a business ever logs. But when the goal is describing typical variability, the range can badly mislead you, especially in small data sets where a single unusual measurement dominates the calculation entirely. Two data sets can even share the exact same range while looking nothing alike in the middle, one tightly clustered and the other spread evenly across the whole interval, because the range has no way to see what happens between the maximum and the minimum.

Because of this weakness, statisticians generally prefer measures that use more of the data set at once, such as the interquartile range, which trims away the extreme top and bottom portions before measuring width, or the standard deviation, which incorporates every value's distance from the mean. The range remains useful as a fast sanity check, an easy number to report alongside more careful measures, and a clear illustration of why spread, like center, needs both a resistant and a non-resistant tool in your kit.

It helps to keep the range in the same mental category as the mean: both are easy to compute, both use extreme or evenly weighted information rather than resisting it, and both can be thrown off badly by a single unusual data point. Just as you would not report a mean income without at least checking the median, you should not report a range without asking whether the maximum or minimum might be an outlier rather than a genuine, representative part of the data set.
